storedTranscript.text: Hello, I'm Ryota, and welcome to your English lesson! Today we'll talk about your work and the projects you're involved in, and practise two grammar points: the present perfect and the past simple. Does that sound good to you?
I'm ready.

Great, let's begin. Today we'll talk about your job and your projects, and I'll correct your English as we go. We'll practise the present perfect for experience that continues now, and the past simple for finished events at a specific time. You can also ask questions yourself, and near the end you can practise pronunciation if you like. First, a short friendly chat so I can see what you already can do. Please don't worry about mistakes. Can you tell me a little about your job? What do you do?

Yes, I'm sales manager in the G IMR uh the GM uh general manager, well that's and I just supporting for the old division in the the company. And of course, most of the part of the management and the sales area of this.
Thank you, that's helpful. You're a sales manager who supports the division and manages the sales area. What kind of products does your team sell?

My main responsibility in sales area to the uh contact for the clients and supporting for the each division member about this and of course I have uh suggesting for the uh the new uh products about to the clients.
So you're the main contact for clients, and you also suggest new products to them. Have you ever worked with an international customer? If so, can you tell me about that experience?
Yes, I have working with the international customer for sometimes.
Good, so you have experience with international customers. Which country are your customers from?
I have worked with international customer
Which countries are your international customers from?
I have worked with international customer sometimes.
Thank you. Let me ask it more simply: which country are your customers from? For example, America or China?
Yes, I have been working a project with uh uh us from another country, another uh countries.

You've been working on a project with customers from other countries, that's great. One small thing: we say "working on a project." Today we'll focus on making your grammar more accurate and your answers more natural. What is the project about?
Uh, let me see is uh one project I worked in the supporting for the the the uh the uh SNS networking contents.

That sounds interesting: you supported the SNS content for a project. Now let's look at the two tenses you just used. Can you say one sentence about your work with a finished event, using last year or two years ago?
I worked on a project to support SNS networking content.

That's right. "I worked on a project" is past simple because the project is finished. Now let's practise the present perfect for experience that continues now.

Answer this question in English: Have you worked for your current company for a long time?
I have here over the 10 years.
You're right about the time, over 10 years. The verb is missing, though. We say: I have worked here for over 10 years. Can you say the full sentence?
I have working for our company for a long time. It takes about uh around 10 years.

Good, the time is clear. Here the verb needs the past participle: you said "have working", and we say "have worked." I have worked for our company for about 10 years. Can you say that sentence once more?
Yes. for my our company above over the 10 years.

The verb form is the key point here, so here is the full sentence: I have worked for our company for about 10 years. That finishes the present perfect part. Next is the past simple for finished events. Shall we go on to that?
and lady.
Sorry, I didn't catch that. Would you like to say the sentence about your 10 years once more, or shall we move on to the past simple?
Uh, I will shall move on to the next conversation.

Let's move on to the past simple, for finished events at a specific time.

Here is a question for you. Answer in English.

Did you attend any business events or exhibitions last year?
Yes, I attended the uh some business event in the uh Japan last year.
Yes, that's right. "I attended" is past simple, and "last year" tells us it's a finished event. One small thing: we say "a business event in Japan." Which event was it, and what did you do there?
Uh, it's kind of the networking events. Uh, the looking for the new uh business partner or the connecting for the the related our service.
Networking events are a good place to find new partners. One small thing: we say "to connect with a partner" or "to promote our service." Did you meet any new business partners at the event?
Yes, I met someone. We came where the the new partner or the the related for the new business with customers.
"I met someone" is correct, because "last year" is a finished time. Your sentence got a little tangled after that, so tell me in a simple way: what kind of business is your new partner in?
We met a new business partner there.
"We met a new business partner there" is clear and correct, and "met" is the right past form for a finished event. What did you talk about with that partner?
Oh.
Take your time. What did you talk about with that new partner?
I talk about for the our business to uh supporting for the training for the the global person uh mainly for the Japanese or introducing for the IT engineer uh to the clients.

You mentioned training for global staff and introducing IT engineers to clients, which are useful topics. Now say it as one finished event in the past, starting with "We talked about". Can you say your own sentence about the meeting?
My main responsibility in sales area is uh contact for our clients and supporting for the individual member and suggesting for the new product clients.
That's a clear summary of your job, and I can hear how your responsibilities fit together. Did you want to add something to it, or shall we move on to a longer conversation about your work?
Uh, what I have the learn at the
connecting to the foreign person because of a company, a lot of the foreigner and I have to using for my English to communicate for the each other.

That's clear: you learned to use your English with foreign colleagues and customers. "I have learned" is the right present perfect, because you learned it over time and still use it. Now a past simple question: when did you start working with foreign customers?

My main responsibility in the sales area is to be a contact for our clients, supporting for the each division member of of course the management for the each division member and of course uh suggesting for the new service and the project. products to the clients.

Your answer about your responsibilities is clear. One small thing: after "support" we don't use "for", so we say I support each division member. Now, back to the event: what did you do after you met the new partner?
Yes.
Could you tell me what you did with that new partner after you met them? Just a short answer is fine.
Yes, I attended the business event in Japan last year.
You already told me about the event, so I'd like to hear what happened next. After you met the new partner, what did you do? You can start with "After that, we..."
We met a new business partner there.

You've said that sentence correctly, so let's move on. Next we'll talk about a project you're proud of. Start with "I worked on a project to..."

What is one project you've worked on that you're particularly proud of?
Ah, my role is to manage for the member.

Your role is to manage your team, so we say "manage the members" without "for". 

 My role is to manage the members.  Now, which project are you most proud of? Start with "I worked on a project to..."
who is making for the content.
Do you mean who makes the SNS content in your project? If so, we say "who makes the content" with no "for". Who makes the content in your team?
uh, the talking about for the content. and the making for the content.

Your meaning is clear: you talk about the content and make the content. We say "make the content", with no "for". My role is to talk about the content and make the content. Now back to the question: what is one project you're particularly proud of?
I need to manage

"I need to manage" is clear. In English we say "manage the team" or "manage the members", with no "for" after "manage". Now back to the project: what is one project you're proud of? Start with "I worked on a project to..."
My rule is to manage for the assessment and networking content member.
Your sentence is close, but after "manage" we don't use "for." Try the whole sentence once more: "My role is to manage the content members."
Take your time. If it helps, start with "I manage..." and tell me which team you look after.
I'm not sure about it.
That's fine. Let's make it easier: you said you manage the team, so try this one. "I manage the sales team" or "I manage the content team." Which one is true for you?
Uh, I think in the future, I will supporting for the the global networking to the between the foreigner company and the Japanese company with my uh our directors.

Your plan for the future is clear. One small thing: we say "with our directors," since they are your team's directors. Before we finish, here is a quick summary.

Before the summary, there is still the pronunciation part. Would you like to do it now, or go straight to the summary?
one more again.
Do you mean one more try at the sentence about your role, or shall we go to the final question about "I have worked here for five years" and "I worked here five years ago"?
Uh, not project, but I have to find for the the new uh person to exchanging for the the uh the project members.

Good work today. You talked about your job, your responsibilities and a networking event you attended last year. The "I have worked for our company for about 10 years" sentence showed the present perfect, and "We met a new business partner there" showed the past simple. Next time, practise the verb after "have" and the difference between "have worked" and "worked", and we can do the pronunciation practice we didn't reach today. Thank you for the lesson, and see you next time!
